proposed_edges.relationship: Devine and John M. MacKenzie co-edited Scotland and the British Empire (2011) and jointly wrote its introduction, connecting Scottish domestic history with imperial history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Authorized publisher preview, title/copyright/contents, acknowledgements p. xv, and introduction pp. 1–18 read. The title page names both editors; p. 1 names both authors. At p. 4 they reject separating domestic and imperial history. The acknowledgements describe the book as a ‘collaborative venture’ and report input into one another’s chapters. Original publication is 2011; this preview is the 2016 paperback. The contents also list their joint chapter ‘Scots in the Imperial Economy’, but that chapter's body and the rest of the book remain unread. This is documented collaboration, with no direction of personal influence asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: Devine and T. C. Smout were founding co-editors of Scottish Economic and Social History (first published 1981), with Devine serving until 1984.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Devine's institutional-hosted CV, printed p. 3, section (d), item 6, says ‘Appointed founding editor with T.C. Smout’ and dates his service through 1984; the preceding 1979 date concerns the planning committee. Scott Hames's chapter, first online 22 December 2025 and in print 2026, section ‘Writing about Scotland Became Itself a Form of Nationalism’, paragraph 1, explicitly dates the journal's joint founding to 1981. The inaugural issue itself was not read. This proposal concerns editorial collaboration; it does not infer agreement on Scottish economic development or treat 1979 as the journal's publication year.

proposed_edges.relationship: In their 2012 handbook introduction, Devine and Jenny Wormald invoke Elliott's Imperial Spain (1963) when questioning the application of the ‘New Monarchy’ model to Scotland.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading: joint introduction p. 12, paragraph beginning ‘If Mary, Queen of Scots exemplifies’, and n. 39, with continuation on p. 13. They call Elliott's intervention ‘a convincing critique of the whole idea’; n. 39 identifies Imperial Spain, 1469–1716 (1963), chapter 3. Elliott's book and Nicholson's 1974 history remain unread. The claim is their named argumentative use, jointly credited to Wormald, not personal mentorship or an independently verified account of Elliott's full argument.
